title: Nvidia's DLSS 5 leaked early, and modders have already broken it out of its Blackwell cage

questions.question: Will NVIDIA officially support DLSS 5 on RTX 40-series GPUs by January 31, 2027?
questions.why_it_matters: Official support on RTX 40-series cards would expand DLSS 5’s eligible installed base beyond RTX 50-series owners, potentially increasing adoption and the value of NVIDIA’s software ecosystem. The article’s account suggests that RTX 40-series support may be technically possible, but does not establish that NVIDIA will provide it.
questions.why_not_already_covered: The existing question about launching DLSS 5 tracks the product’s launch, not which GPU generations NVIDIA officially supports. DLSS 5 could launch on RTX 50-series cards while remaining unsupported on RTX 40-series cards, or NVIDIA could extend official support later; those outcomes can differ independently.
questions.how_and_when_to_check: Check by January 31, 2027, an analyst check date at NVIDIA’s FY2027 year-end; the article gives no date for an RTX 40-series support decision. Review NVIDIA’s official DLSS 5 compatibility documentation, release notes, announcements, and supported-game or driver materials for explicit RTX 40-series support. A modded or unofficial workaround alone would not resolve whether NVIDIA officially supports it.

evidence.quote: Nvidia's official position is Blackwell only, and the leaked DLL behaved that way.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article describes NVIDIA’s stated support position as limited to Blackwell, evidence against official RTX 40-series support at the time of publication.
evidence.original_speaker: The article’s journalist, describing NVIDIA’s official position.

evidence.quote: It was never a hardware wall. The model runs on FP8, which Ada Lovelace supports natively, and the real block was a set of CUDA binaries only RTX 50 series cards could read.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article’s explanation suggests that RTX 40-series support may be technically feasible despite the current software restriction; it does not say NVIDIA has committed to enable it.

evidence.quote: RTX Remix modder Uncle Burrito swapped them out, saying he identified the binaries incompatible with Ada and patched in fresh ones himself.
evidence.what_it_shows: A modder reportedly worked around the incompatibility. This supports the possibility of RTX 40-series operation, but the workaround is not evidence of NVIDIA’s official support.
evidence.original_speaker: The article, reporting what RTX Remix modder Uncle Burrito said.

evidence.quote: The fix has been verified working on an RTX 4080, with other versions in progress.
evidence.what_it_shows: The reported workaround works on at least one RTX 40-series card, suggesting potential reach to that generation; it does not establish official NVIDIA support or a commitment to provide it.

evidence.quote: Ampere is a much harder problem, since those cards have no native FP8 support to fall back on.
evidence.what_it_shows: The article distinguishes the RTX 40-series workaround from the harder technical challenge on an older GPU generation, helping clarify the scope of the potential compatibility extension.

judgements.reasons: The reference is NVIDIA's stated position at the time of publication—Blackwell only—which sits at rung 2 (No); no separate market consensus is supplied. The evidence supports that outcome through the check date: there is no reported NVIDIA commitment or official support change, while the RTX 40-series result is an unofficial workaround. The evidence of technical feasibility modestly raises the chance of a later change, but does not outweigh the stated restriction or establish official support, so the forecast does not cross to rung 1.
judgements.implied_outcome: Most likely, NVIDIA still will not officially support DLSS 5 on RTX 40-series GPUs by January 31, 2027. The reported official restriction remains Blackwell-only; technical feasibility and a working RTX 4080 modded workaround do not establish an official support change.

article:
Nvidia's DLSS 5 was supposed to land this fall, on RTX 50 series cards, in games Nvidia had chosen. It arrived early instead, inside a basketball game nobody was watching for graphics leaks. The early access build of NBA 2K27 shipped with a 158MB library called nvngx_dlssnr.dll, roughly three times the size of its DLSS 4 equivalent, carrying the runtime for Neural Rendering. VideoCardz spotted the file first and noted there was no obvious way to use it outside Nvidia's own implementation. That held for a few hours. The RenoDX modding community had the library running inside Control the same day, forcing it into a game Nvidia never intended it for, with seven selectable styles and the effect landing on character models only.
Modders got further in two days than Nvidia's own launch schedule
Elden Ring, The Last of Us Part II and Skyrim followed quickly. So did A Hat in Time, a DirectX 9 platformer with no place anywhere near Nvidia's launch lineup. Part of why it spread so fast is that Neural Rendering seems to want the same inputs regular DLSS upscaling already receives, which makes Unreal Engine 5 titles the obvious next target for anyone with a Discord account and some patience.
The frame rate cost makes this unusable in its current state
One RenoDX developer measured Control on an RTX 5070 Ti at 4K dropping from 71fps to 35fps with the effect enabled, and described the build as effectively unusable.
Reports across other titles put the hit somewhere between 40 and 60 percent. HDR is broken too, so most testing is happening in SDR while developers work out what the model expects from its image data. There is a structural reason for the cost. The Neural Rendering pass currently runs late in the pipeline, after upscaling and possibly after tone mapping, which is almost certainly not where the shipping version will sit.
The RTX 50 series requirement turned out to be software, not silicon
Nvidia's official position is Blackwell only, and the leaked DLL behaved that way. It was never a hardware wall. The model runs on FP8, which Ada Lovelace supports natively, and the real block was a set of CUDA binaries only RTX 50 series cards could read. RTX Remix modder Uncle Burrito swapped them out, saying he identified the binaries incompatible with Ada and patched in fresh ones himself. The fix has been verified working on an RTX 4080, with other versions in progress. Ampere is a much harder problem, since those cards have no native FP8 support to fall back on. The result is a very public preview Nvidia did not ask for. Jesse Faden is about 28 in Control and emerges from Neural Rendering looking middle-aged. The rigs and animations underneath stay untouched, so newly photoreal faces blink and turn like 2019 assets, which is where most of the uncanny effect comes from. Nvidia has spent since March fending off accusations that DLSS 5 smears AI slop across games, and re-pitched it in July as a tool that respects artistic intent. Per scene and per object developer controls are meant to be the proof. None of that exists in a DLL bolted onto Skyrim, and that is the version everyone is judging right now.
